To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the percent oil recovery as determined from the model system is in reasonable agreement with the percent oil recovery that would be obtained if all of the nonadsorbed, post-cac surfactant were present at the oil-water-copper interface and that the percent oil removal by solubilization plus emulsification is determined by the oil-water interfacially tension of the nonadsorbable, post-cac AOT solution.
the contact angle between the oil, water, and calcium carbonate surfaces is the dominant parameter controlling oil recovery by surfacant solutions.

the oil recovery by flooding a calcium carbonate-packed column with an aqueous solution of anionic surfactants increases with increasing surfactant concentration, and the increase occurs in two distinct regions: a region of low surfactant concentration where oil recovery is determined by the oil-water contact angle, and a region of high surfactant concentration above the critical aggregation point where oil recovery is due to a combination of emulsification and solubilization plus mobilization due to a low oil-water interphase
In summary, our research is concerned with
a detailed characterization of model systems of surfactant solution injection into porous media and a comparison of the measured results with theoretical predictions.
the study of the behavior of model systems of oil, water, and surfactant in porous media.
the development of a quantitative model for surfactant flooding of porous media.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the percent oil recovery is determined by the oil-water interfacially tension, the contact angle, and the adsorption of surfactant onto the solid surface.
the model system studied here is a reasonable representation of the behavior of an actual porous medium.

the oil recovery behavior of the model systems is in reasonable agreement with that predicted by the theory of the oil recovery process, and that the model systems are therefore a good model of the oil recovery behavior in porous media.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in general, the percent oil recovery increases with the surfactant's cac and decreases with the oil-water interfacially tension.

the percent oil recovery as measured by pumping AOT solution into a calcium carbonate-packed column initially filled with oil is determined by the oil-water interfaciai tension, which is in turn determined by the AOT concentration.

the percent oil recovery is a function of the post-cac oilwater interfacial tension, the oil-water-copper oxide contact angle, the adsorption of AOT onto the oil-water and water-calcium oxide interfaces, the AOT solubility, and the pumping pressure increase due to the low interfacial tension.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, although the oil recovery behavior of our model systems is in qualitative accord with the theoretical predictions of the literature, there are important differences between our results and the theory which are due mainly to the effects of surfactant adsorption on the calcium carbonate-water and oil-water surfaces.

the percent oil recovery is determined by the oil-water contact angle for surfactant concentrations below the cac, while above the cac the percent recovery is determined by a combination of low oil-water inter-facial tension and pumping pressure increase.
the oil recovery behavior of the model systems is in good agreement with the predictions of the theory of oil displacement by aqueous surfactants.
